title: Abdominal closure with unresolved bowel viability
clarityIssues: 'Scattered areas remain grey and do not contract' does not distinguish questionable viability suitable for reassessment from frankly nonviable bowel requiring treatment before any closure decision. The explanation assumes the former without settling that distinction.
The current update supplies enough operative history to understand this remaining node without the parked earlier questions. The presentation's chest findings are now extraneous.

cues.phrase: the abdominal wall has no tissue loss
cues.why: This particularly weakens 'Skin closure with deferred fascial reconstruction'; that option is a poor competitor in an abdomen whose fascia also approximates easily. This is option-specific elimination, not a reliable nonmedical route to the key.

fairness: Temporary closure is a plausible best wall plan when a second-look assessment of uncertain intestinal viability remains necessary despite recovered systemic physiology. The competing favorable closure findings create a real interpretation/application conflict.

The supplied observations also raise the possibility of dead bowel. This is an unresolved clinical interpretation, not a finding that temporary closure is inherently wrong. The explanation must not imply that leaving clearly nonviable bowel is an adequate treatment.
No defensible exact perfusion threshold can be inferred from the fictional temperature, pH or color descriptions.

High-yield objective: indications for maintaining an open abdomen and the limits of physiologic recovery as a closure criterion. Difficulty is predicted, not measured; this offline review confers no clinical approval.
suggestions: Clarify the actual intraoperative viability assessment and what has been done about unequivocally nonviable tissue before asking the wall decision. Use supported observations, not a pre-answer statement that a second look is required.
Have the clinician distinguish the remaining indeterminate segment from established necrosis and explain that distinction after the answer.
Replace the weak deferred-reconstruction foil with a credible same-stage closure strategy if one can be supported; do not pad the option set or erase the favorable fascial-approximation findings.

title: Evolving symptoms after equivocal bowel-trauma CT
fairness: Repeat contrast-enhanced CT is the best of the offered plans: the resident must recognize a worsening trajectory after nonspecific initial findings, then distinguish the need for renewed investigation from either unchanged observation or immediate exploration.

The current update states the prior CT, elapsed interval, examination and hemodynamics. It stands alone and follows coherently from the preserved observation node. That earlier explanation recommends serial assessment but does not supply the repeat-CT answer.

The soft abdomen and absent involuntary guarding/rebound are necessary discrimination data, not gratuitous deletion of surgical danger signs. Increasing tenderness and tachycardia make unchanged serial examination a credible but less appropriate alternative.
No material wording, length, convergence, diagnostic-label or absolute-language shortcut identified. The prior CT is not a disposable foil: evolving findings give a reason to repeat it.

High-yield concept: recognition and reassessment of occult blunt bowel injury. The six-hour interval is case chronology, not a gameplay wait or a universal deadline. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in this offline review; PASS is editorial only.
suggestions: Retain the trajectory and decision-critical examination findings. In clinician sign-off, confirm the intended boundary between repeat imaging and exploration without converting these fictional observations into numeric treatment thresholds.

title: Recurrent bile collection after catheter displacement
clarityIssues: The recurrent collection and failed catheter communication are clear. The CT description and injection record largely prove the same mechanical problem twice.

cues.phrase: The catheter curl lies in abdominal-wall tissue rather than inside the fluid.
cues.why: Even without clinical knowledge, an out-of-position drain points directly to the only replacement-drain option. This supplies almost the entire mechanical inference.

cues.phrase: Image-guided placement of a replacement collection drain
cues.why: 'Replacement' uniquely repairs the explicitly described misplaced catheter; the other options address different structures or a broader space.

cues.phrase: The cavity abuts the lateral wall along a path without intervening bowel or pleura
cues.why: The detailed safe-access description rehearses the percutaneous option's feasibility after its indication is already obvious.

cues.phrase: the deep fluid cavity does not opacify
cues.why: This duplicates the CT's explicit loss of catheter-cavity communication rather than adding a consequential second decision.

fairness: Replacing the drain is clinically coherent and best among these choices for the described localized, accessible recurrent collection. ERCP may address a continuing duct leak but does not substitute for drainage of the current infected cavity.
The prior liver nodes concern observation and arterial bleeding; their explanations do not disclose the drain-replacement answer. This update supplies its own drainage history and can stand alone.
The problem is difficulty and overdetermination, not an identified wrong key. Removing the earlier bile-culture narrative would still leave an almost direct mechanical replacement task.
Source control of traumatic bile collections is high yield, but this exact item mostly tests noticing that a drain is outside its target. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline.
suggestions: Build the decision around a real, supported competition between inadequate cavity drainage and a persistent biliary leak, with observations that must be integrated to determine the initial procedure.
Use one adequate catheter-position/communication record; avoid duplicating the same answer-defining observation.
Retain clinically necessary accessibility and stability information, but avoid stacking a uniquely feasible key against clearly mismatched procedures.
If this mechanical-recognition version is retained, request an explicitly accepted foundational role instead of calling it a difficult two-step resident item.

title: Adequacy of bladder imaging after pelvic trauma
fairness: Retrograde CT cystography is the best offered study. The resident must infer that persistent gross hematuria with pelvic fracture needs bladder evaluation, then recognize that excreted contrast in an underfilled bladder does not supply an adequate cystogram.

The acquisition log establishes what was actually obtained; the item does not equate a missing exported image with a missing acquisition. Upper-tract opacification explains why simply extending an excretory CT pathway is the closest protocol error.
The catheter history makes routine retrograde urethrography a weaker initial answer without asserting that easy catheter passage or absent meatal blood absolutely excludes urethral injury.

'Bladder walls remain apposed' and 'bladder distension' are related, but interpreting their diagnostic significance requires protocol knowledge. No independent nonmedical wording shortcut strong enough to determine the answer was identified.

The node is self-contained. Its explanation teaches acquisition adequacy, not the following node's repair exception. This is a high-yield trauma-imaging distinction. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline; PASS is editorial only.
suggestions: Preserve the actual acquisition record and distinguish inadequate bladder evaluation from a negative result.
Do not expand the explanation into an absolute rule excluding urethral injury from the catheter observations.

title: Extraperitoneal bladder injury complicated by a bone fragment
fairness: Primary repair with urethral catheter drainage is the best offered plan. The resident must interpret the extraperitoneal leak distribution, then recognize that intraluminal bone makes the usual catheter-only approach inappropriate.

The urethral-catheter plan is a credible default for an uncomplicated extraperitoneal injury. Switching to suprapubic drainage does not remove the penetrating fragment, so it is a weaker but distinct management error.

The raw bony finding is decisive and must remain; it is not a diagnosis label or a wording match to the key. Options are parallel concrete bladder plans, with no uniquely long key, absolute-language cue or majority-component shortcut.

The update restates circulation, catheter function and current tests. It follows the preceding imaging question coherently and stands alone. Prior feedback about cystographic adequacy does not teach this treatment exception.

High-yield distinction: complicated versus uncomplicated extraperitoneal bladder trauma. The stale 'intraperitoneal' identifier is not learner-visible evidence and was not used to infer the answer. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline; PASS is editorial only.
suggestions: In post-answer teaching, explicitly include management of the intraluminal bone fragment as part of repair so the explanation does not imply that closing around it is sufficient.
Preserve the extraperitoneal imaging findings and intact urethral drainage; do not turn the case into a simple intraperitoneal-rupture recall question.

title: Renal trauma imaging despite absent hematuria
clarityIssues: The task calls the patient's 'abdominal and upper urinary tract injuries' established before any diagnostic imaging; the supplied record establishes concern, not confirmed injury.

'No blood in urine' does not specify visible urine appearance versus urinalysis. The explanation interprets it as clear urine. This does not reverse the imaging indication, but it muddies the intended misconception.

cues.phrase: IV-contrast CT with arterial, venous and excretory acquisitions
cues.why: The key is a strict additive superset of 'IV-contrast CT with arterial and venous acquisitions'. A choose-the-most-complete-list strategy favors it without interpreting the clinical findings.

cues.phrase: abdominal and upper urinary tract injuries
cues.why: The broad task preselects comprehensive anatomical coverage. It also makes the kidney-only ultrasound label look incomplete before any medical reasoning.

cues.phrase: Renal ultrasonography with Doppler perfusion assessment
cues.why: This is the only kidney-limited modality against two explicitly abdominal/upper-tract CT protocols, reinforcing the coverage shortcut.

fairness: A contrast CT protocol that includes urinary excretory assessment is a plausible best answer given high-energy deceleration and flank findings despite absent visible hematuria.

The question does not convincingly require two consequential steps: even after removing the no-hematuria and FAST findings, the most comprehensive CT option remains readily favored by the task and option structure.
The later renal-leak node follows coherently, and the initial explanation does not reveal its management answer. This first node stands alone.

The imaging indication and delayed urinary-phase concept are high yield. This review does not establish that exactly three separately acquired phases are universally mandatory; protocol specifics need clinician/source confirmation. No confident wrong-key finding is asserted.
suggestions: Use a neutral task about evaluation after the recorded trauma, without presupposing diagnosed upper-tract injury.
Specify whether hematuria is absent macroscopically or on urinalysis when that distinction is part of the objective.
Rebuild the choices around a clinically meaningful acquisition or adequacy decision, using equally scoped plans whose ranking depends on the findings rather than a longer inclusive list.

Retain the deceleration/flank evidence and the legitimate lesson that absent hematuria does not exclude significant injury. Do not manufacture contrast contraindications or arbitrary imaging cutoffs to create difficulty.

title: Persistent obstruction despite a smaller duodenal hematoma
clarityIssues: 'Sixteen days later' clearly locates the decision, but the smaller collection and improved pain coexist with unchanged functional obstruction. The intended clinical boundary for abandoning conservative treatment is not fully established by the explanation.

cues.phrase: The D2/D3 intramural collection is smaller, but marked luminal narrowing and upstream distension remain.
cues.why: The 'but' construction directs attention toward treatment failure, although the actual imaging/function conflict still requires clinical interpretation. This is a mild emphasis cue, not a sufficient nonmedical answer shortcut.

fairness: The item earns two steps: distinguish anatomical improvement from persistent functional obstruction, then choose whether and how to escalate. Both continued decompression and evacuation are credible considerations; bypass is less attractive with preserved wall anatomy.

The unresolved issue is whether operative evacuation is uniquely best now in this stable, improving-imaging patient, rather than one supported option after a prolonged course. I am not confident that day 16 plus the supplied findings makes continued decompression indefensible. This is a clinical-ranking uncertainty, not a proven incorrect key or an invented deadline.
The explanation says escalation 'is supported', which does not itself establish superiority over the closest offered alternative. No source was retrieved during this offline review.

The current node stands alone. The next node's discovery of a separate D2 tear is possible after negative CT findings, but its chronology and containment need to be made explicit there; negative imaging is not proof that a later operative tear cannot exist.
Persistent obstruction after traumatic duodenal hematoma is a high-yield concept, though the exact escalation boundary is more conditional than simple hematoma recognition.
suggestions: Have the named clinician verify that this exact persistent functional course establishes a best next intervention over further observation; explain the patient-specific ranking rather than implying a universal day-based rule.
If the evidence only supports considering intervention, revise the decision point or options so the question does not present that conditional recommendation as mandatory.
Preserve the disagreement between smaller imaging size and unchanged passage. Do not manufacture deterioration, an exact output threshold or a fixed treatment deadline merely to force a key.

title: Repair of a viable localized D2 defect
clarityIssues: The current update says 'exploration for persistent obstruction' but omits the sixteen-day interval supplied in the earlier node. The explanation invokes 'delayed discovery', so the potentially consequential delay disappears when this node is encountered alone.

A separate D2 tear with localized bile staining appears after a repeat CT described no leak or gas. This is not inherently contradictory, but the record does not say whether the tear was a contained missed traumatic defect or arose during the current procedure.

cues.phrase: Temporary edge approximation needs no traction and leaves the lumen similar in caliber to the adjacent uninjured duodenum.
cues.why: This essentially demonstrates successful local closure before the resident selects the primary-repair option. It strongly rehearses the keyed rationale rather than making a second decision consequential.

cues.phrase: The ampulla, distal bile duct and pancreatic head are intact.
cues.why: Together with small extent, bleeding edges, easy approximation and favorable physiology, the stem stacks favorable repair criteria against escalation. These are legitimate safety/anatomy observations, but the complete bundle leaves little meaningful competition.

fairness: Primary transverse repair is a plausible best answer for the supplied viable, limited, approximable defect. I identify no confident clinical error in that key.

Resection and routine pyloric exclusion are much less compelling when every current observation favors direct repair. As a standalone node this mainly applies a single repair-feasibility rule; the claimed conflict with delay depends on omitted prior chronology.

In the sequence, the earlier feedback does not directly give the repair answer. However, it establishes the prolonged course that this explanation relies on, so standalone difficulty differs from sequential difficulty.

Defect geometry, viability and selective use of more extensive duodenal procedures are high yield. Anatomical complexity or delayed presentation should not be asserted to require exclusion without evidence.
suggestions: State the relevant elapsed interval and whether the defect was contained before discovery in this node's own update; clarify its origin without implying that negative CT excludes a traumatic tear.
Reassess the option competition after making the delay explicit. Use a supported competing clinical consideration rather than merely adding more favorable primary-repair criteria.
Retain the observations needed to show that primary repair is safe; do not remove decisive safety data to make the item harder.
If a genuinely competing decision cannot be supported, seek an accepted foundational role rather than claiming a difficult two-step application.

title: Small jejunal defect with adjacent mesenteric devascularization
fairness: Resection with immediate anastomosis is the best offered plan. The small antimesenteric opening initially favors direct repair, but the torn mesentery and persistently nonviable-appearing adjacent bowel change the required extent of treatment.

The second consequential decision is reconstruction now versus staged discontinuity: perfused bowel beyond the injured segment, controlled bleeding, recovered physiology and lack of marked edema or diffuse soilage support immediate anastomosis.

The two resection choices prevent recognition of devascularization from completing the entire task. All options name the same jejunal site and are comparably specific; no material lexical, length, convergence or absolute-language shortcut identified.
The findings are deliberately decisive but clinically necessary. Do not misclassify all normal physiology as cueing when it distinguishes the deferred-reconstruction alternative.

This is a self-contained single-node case with a complete task. It tests high-yield small-bowel trauma decisions about viability and reconstruction. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline; PASS is editorial only.
suggestions: Retain the conflict between a small wall defect and a larger perfusion injury, as well as the separate reconstruction evidence.
Keep the fictional physiologic values as observations rather than presenting them as universal thresholds for anastomosis.
